Course Overview & Syllabus Mapping
Welcome to 22AIE463: Time Series Analysis, an advanced core course in the Artificial Intelligence and Computer Science Engineering curriculum at Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham.
Time series analysis occupies a distinct, foundational position at the intersection of mathematical statistics, dynamical systems theory, signal processing, and machine learning. In conventional statistical learning, observations are almost universally assumed to be independent and identically distributed (\(i.i.d.\)). In the physical universe, however, time flows monotonically in a single direction; the past casts an enduring shadow upon the present, and the present constrains the future. When observations are temporally correlated, standard estimators collapse, standard errors evaporate into spurious precision, and regression lines mistake persistence for causality.
This coursebook is formulated from first principles, weaving rigorous mathematical derivations into an intuitive narrative strictly anchored in the prescribed curriculum textbooks [1], [2], [3], [4]. Every chapter advances systematically from theoretical foundations to graduated analytical problems, culminating in comprehensive laboratory experiments utilizing real-world open datasets.

Course Information

Course Code: 22AIE463
Course Title: Time Series Analysis
Structure (L-T-P-C): 2-0-3- 3 (2 Lecture hours, 0 Tutorial hours, 3 Practical/Lab hours per week; 3 Credits)
Target Audience: B.Tech Artificial Intelligence and Data Science / Computer Science Engineering


Course Objectives

Cover fundamental mathematical tools and statistical techniques required to analyze, filter, and model temporally dependent stochastic processes.
Establish unified theoretical foundations for both linear (AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA, SARIMA, VAR) and nonlinear time series analysis (TAR, STAR, State-Space, ARCH/GARCH).
Develop advanced predictive analytics capabilities utilizing Machine Learning (tree ensembles, sliding window feature engineering) and Deep Learning (LSTM, GRU, TCN, Attention/Transformers).
Investigate mathematical early warning indicators and precursors for catastrophic transitions (bifurcations and tipping points) in complex dynamical systems.



Course Outcomes (COs)
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

CO1: Formulate, analyze, estimate, and evaluate linear time series models from first mathematical principles.
CO2: Mathematically characterize, detect, and model nonlinear dynamics and conditional heteroscedastic phenomena.
CO3: Rigorously analyze stationary and non-stationary stochastic processes using formal hypothesis testing frameworks.
CO4: Design, implement, and benchmark modern Machine Learning and Deep Learning architectures for temporal predictive analytics and tipping-point detection.

Mathematical Notational Conventions
Throughout this text, we maintain rigorous notational consistency:

\((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\) denotes the underlying probability space.
\(\{X_t\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}\) or \(\{Y_t\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}\) denotes a discrete-time stochastic process.
\(\mathbb{E}[X]\) denotes the mathematical expectation of random variable \(X\).
\(\gamma(s, t) = \mathrm{Cov}(X_s, X_t) = \mathbb{E}[(X_s - \mu_s)(X_t - \mu_t)]\) denotes the autocovariance function. For weakly stationary processes, \(\gamma(h) = \mathrm{Cov}(X_t, X_{t+h})\).
\(\rho(h) = \frac{\gamma(h)}{\gamma(0)}\) denotes the autocorrelation function (ACF) at lag \(h\).
\(\alpha(h)\) or \(\phi_{hh}\) denotes the partial autocorrelation function (PACF) at lag \(h\).
\(B\) (or \(L\)) denotes the backward shift (lag) operator, such that \(B^k X_t = X_{t-k}\).
\(\nabla = (1 - B)\) denotes the first-difference operator: \(\nabla X_t = X_t - X_{t-1}\).
\(\{W_t\}\) or \(\{Z_t\}\) or \(\{\epsilon_t\}\) denotes a white noise innovation sequence with mean zero and variance \(\sigma^2\), denoted \(WN(0, \sigma^2)\) or \(i.i.d. \, \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\).
\(\Phi(B) = 1 - \phi_1 B - \dots - \phi_p B^p\) denotes the autoregressive characteristic polynomial.
\(\Theta(B) = 1 + \theta_1 B + \dots + \theta_q B^q\) denotes the moving average characteristic polynomial.







[1] J. D. Cryer and K.-S. Chan, Time series analysis: With applications in r, 2nd ed. New York, NY: Springer, 2008. doi: 10.1007/978-0-387-75959-3.


[2] R. H. Shumway and D. S. Stoffer, Time series analysis and its applications: With r examples, 3rd ed. New York, NY: Springer, 2011. doi: 10.1007/978-1-4419-7865-3.


[3] G. E. P. Box, G. M. Jenkins, G. C. Reinsel, and G. M. Ljung, Time series analysis: Forecasting and control, 5th ed. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2016.


[4] A. Nielsen, Practical time series analysis: Prediction with statistics and machine learning, 1st ed. Sebastopol, CA: O’Reilly Media, 2019.

1.1 Opening: Two Signals, One Mathematical Backbone
Imagine two completely different rooms on the same Tuesday morning:
On the surface, brainwaves and stock prices have nothing in common. Underneath, both are ordered sequences indexed by time, and both violate the #1 assumption of introductory statistics:
To analyze the time series data rigorously, we need a shared mathematical backbone. Each section below introduces the key definitions, first-principles derivations, worked sample problems, and key takeaways you need before entering Unit 1.

text:
The Neurology Lab: A clinician places electrodes on a patient’s scalp to record an electroencephalogram (EEG). Every 4 milliseconds (\(250\text{ Hz}\)), the amplifier logs a voltage in microvolts (\(\mu\text{V}\)). When the patient closes their eyes and relaxes, the trace settles into a smooth \(10\text{ Hz}\) ripple—the alpha rhythm. Seconds before an epileptic seizure, that rhythm changes character.
The Trading Desk: A quantitative analyst watches the closing prices of an equity index—say, the NIFTY 50 or S&P 500—alongside trading volume and interest rates. Tomorrow’s portfolio risk depends on whether today’s sudden \(3\%\) drop is an isolated shock or the start of a turbulent volatility cluster.



The \(i.i.d.\) Trap: Standard statistics assumes rows in a dataset are independent and identically distributed (\(i.i.d.\)). If you shuffle the rows of a housing-price table, nothing breaks. If you shuffle the rows of an EEG recording or a stock chart, you destroy the physics of the problem—causality, momentum, cycles, and memory [4].

text:
1.2 Probability & Moment Algebra From Scratch
Almost every proof in Units 1–4 relies on four algebraic rules for random variables. Mastering them now makes every later derivation transparent [1].

1.2.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

Random Variable (\(X\)): A numerical outcome of a random phenomenon (e.g., tomorrow’s return or the EEG voltage at \(t = 1.2\text{ s}\)).
Expectation (\(\mathbb{E}[X]\) or \(\mu_X\)): The probability-weighted average (center of mass) of \(X\): \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_x x \, p(x)\) (discrete) or \(\int_{-\infty}^\infty x f(x)\,dx\) (continuous).
Variance (\(\mathrm{Var}(X)\) or \(\sigma_X^2\)): The expected squared deviation from the mean, measuring spread around \(\mu_X\).
Covariance (\(\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)\)): A measure of the linear co-movement between two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\).
Pearson Correlation (\(\rho(X, Y)\)): A unitless, standardized version of covariance bounded in \([-1, 1]\).



1.2.2 First-Principles Derivations of Moment Identities
Let \(X, Y\) be random variables with finite second moments (\(\mathbb{E}[X^2] < \infty, \mathbb{E}[Y^2] < \infty\)), and let \(a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}\) be constants.

1.2.2.1 Theorem 0.1: Linearity of Expectation & Variance Scaling

\(\mathbb{E}[aX + bY + c] = a\mathbb{E}[X] + b\mathbb{E}[Y] + c\) (holds even when \(X\) and \(Y\) are dependent).
\(\mathrm{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2\).
\(\mathrm{Var}(aX + c) = a^2 \mathrm{Var}(X)\).

Derivation from First Principles: By definition, \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mu_X)^2]\). Expanding the square inside the expectation and applying linearity: \[\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Var}(X) &= \mathbb{E}[X^2 - 2\mu_X X + \mu_X^2] \\
&= \mathbb{E}[X^2] - 2\mu_X \mathbb{E}[X] + \mu_X^2 = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - 2\mu_X^2 + \mu_X^2 = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu_X^2
\end{aligned} \tag{0.1}\] For \(W = aX + c\), its mean is \(\mu_W = \mathbb{E}[aX + c] = a\mu_X + c\). Therefore: \[\mathrm{Var}(aX + c) = \mathbb{E}\big[((aX + c) - (a\mu_X + c))^2\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[a^2(X - \mu_X)^2\big] = a^2 \mathrm{Var}(X) \tag{0.2}\] Adding a constant \(c\) shifts the location but leaves the spread untouched.


1.2.2.2 Theorem 0.2: Bilinearity of Covariance & Sum-of-Variances Identity
For any random variables \(X_1, \dots, X_m\) and \(Y_1, \dots, Y_n\): \[\mathrm{Cov}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i X_i, \, \sum_{j=1}^n b_j Y_j\right) = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n a_i b_j \, \mathrm{Cov}(X_i, Y_j) \tag{0.3}\] In particular, for two variables \(X\) and \(Y\): \[\mathrm{Var}(X + Y) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y) + 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) \tag{0.4}\]
Derivation from First Principles: Let \(\tilde{X}_i = X_i - \mathbb{E}[X_i]\) and \(\tilde{Y}_j = Y_j - \mathbb{E}[Y_j]\) be the centered variables. By linearity of expectation, \(\sum a_i X_i - \mathbb{E}[\sum a_i X_i] = \sum a_i \tilde{X}_i\). Thus: \[\mathrm{Cov}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i X_i, \, \sum_{j=1}^n b_j Y_j\right) = \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^m a_i \tilde{X}_i\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^n b_j \tilde{Y}_j\right)\right] = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n a_i b_j \, \mathbb{E}[\tilde{X}_i \tilde{Y}_j] = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n a_i b_j \, \mathrm{Cov}(X_i, Y_j)\] Setting \(m = n = 2\), \(Y_i = X_i\), and \(a_1 = a_2 = 1\) gives \(\mathrm{Var}(X_1 + X_2) = \mathrm{Cov}(X_1+X_2, X_1+X_2) = \mathrm{Var}(X_1) + \mathrm{Var}(X_2) + 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X_1, X_2)\).



1.2.3 Sample Problem 0.1 (Moment Algebra)
Statement: Let \(Z_1, Z_2, Z_3\) be uncorrelated white noise shocks with mean \(0\) and variance \(\sigma^2 = 4\). Define \(X_2 = Z_2 + 0.5 Z_1\) and \(X_3 = Z_3 + 0.5 Z_2\). Compute \(\mathbb{E}[X_2]\), \(\mathrm{Var}(X_2)\), \(\mathrm{Cov}(X_2, X_3)\), and \(\rho(X_2, X_3)\).
Solution: 1. Mean: \(\mathbb{E}[X_2] = \mathbb{E}[Z_2] + 0.5\,\mathbb{E}[Z_1] = 0\). 2. Variance: Since \(\mathrm{Cov}(Z_1, Z_2) = 0\), \(\mathrm{Var}(X_2) = \mathrm{Var}(Z_2) + (0.5)^2 \mathrm{Var}(Z_1) = 4 + 0.25(4) = 5\). By symmetry, \(\mathrm{Var}(X_3) = 5\). 3. Covariance: By bilinearity (Eq. 0.3): \[\mathrm{Cov}(X_2, X_3) = \mathrm{Cov}(Z_2 + 0.5 Z_1, Z_3 + 0.5 Z_2) = 0 + 0.5\,\mathrm{Cov}(Z_2, Z_2) + 0 + 0 = 0.5(4) = 2\] 4. Correlation: \(\rho(X_2, X_3) = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X_2, X_3)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X_2)\mathrm{Var}(X_3)}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{5 \cdot 5}} = 0.40\).






Key Takeaway: Section 0.2



Covariance is bilinear: you can pull constants out and expand sums just like ordinary polynomial multiplication. When random variables share a common shock (\(Z_2\)), they become correlated—and \(\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)\) gains the cross-term \(2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)\).

text:
1.3 White Noise: The base of Time Series
Every time series model in this course is built by passing pure, unpredictable randomness through a mathematical filter [2]. We call that pure randomness white noise.

1.3.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms






Definition 0.1: White Noise Process



A sequence \(\{Z_t\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}\) is white noise, denoted \(Z_t \sim WN(0, \sigma^2)\), if:

\(\mathbb{E}[Z_t] = 0\) for all \(t\),
\(\mathrm{Var}(Z_t) = \sigma^2 < \infty\) for all \(t\), and
\(\mathrm{Cov}(Z_t, Z_s) = 0\) whenever \(t \neq s\).

If the \(Z_t\) are also independent and Normally distributed, we write \(Z_t \overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) (Gaussian white noise).



Innovation / Shock (\(Z_t\)): The genuinely new, unpredictable information arriving at time \(t\) (e.g., an unexpected RBI rate decision or thermal electrode noise).



1.3.2 Sample Problem 0.2 (Checking White Noise Properties)
Statement: Let \(Z_t \sim WN(0, \sigma^2)\). Suppose \(Y_t = Z_t - Z_{t-1}\). Is \(\{Y_t\}\) white noise?
Solution: Check condition 3: \(\mathrm{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t-1}) = \mathrm{Cov}(Z_t - Z_{t-1}, Z_{t-1} - Z_{t-2}) = -\mathrm{Var}(Z_{t-1}) = -\sigma^2 \neq 0\). Because lag-1 covariance is non-zero, \(\{Y_t\}\) is not white noise (differencing white noise creates negative correlation).






Key Takeaway: Section 0.3



White noise has zero mean, constant variance, and zero correlation across distinct time points. It is the unpredictable “raw fuel” that drives every AR, MA, ARIMA, and State-Space model.

section: 1.4 Difference Equations & The Backward Shift Operator \(B\)
text:
1.4 Difference Equations & The Backward Shift Operator \(B\)
In calculus, differential equations (\(\frac{dx}{dt} = -\lambda x\)) govern continuous time. In digital EEG amplifiers and daily stock closes, time arrives in discrete ticks \(t = 0, 1, 2, \dots\), so difference equations take center stage [3].

1.4.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

Backward Shift (Lag) Operator (\(B\)): Shifts a series one step back in time: \(B X_t = X_{t-1}\), and in general \(B^k X_t = X_{t-k}\).
First-Difference Operator (\(\nabla\)): Computes the step-to-step change: \(\nabla X_t = (1 - B) X_t = X_t - X_{t-1}\).
Second-Difference Operator (\(\nabla^2\)): \(\nabla^2 X_t = (1 - B)^2 X_t = (1 - 2B + B^2) X_t = X_t - 2X_{t-1} + X_{t-2}\).



1.4.2 First-Principles Derivation: Geometric Inversion of \((1 - \phi B)\)
Consider the first-order linear difference equation \(X_t = \phi X_{t-1} + Z_t\) with \(|\phi| < 1\). Writing \(X_{t-1} = B X_t\): \[(1 - \phi B) X_t = Z_t \tag{0.5}\] How do we solve for \(X_t\) in terms of the shocks \(Z_t\)? By recursive substitution: \[\begin{aligned}
X_t &= \phi X_{t-1} + Z_t = \phi(\phi X_{t-2} + Z_{t-1}) + Z_t \\
&= Z_t + \phi Z_{t-1} + \phi^2 Z_{t-2} + \dots + \phi^{k-1} Z_{t-k+1} + \phi^k X_{t-k}
\end{aligned} \tag{0.6}\] Because \(|\phi| < 1\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X_{t-k})\) is bounded, \(\mathbb{E}[(\phi^k X_{t-k})^2] = \phi^{2k}\mathrm{Var}(X_{t-k}) \to 0\) as \(k \to \infty\). Thus: \[X_t = \frac{1}{1 - \phi B} Z_t = \sum_{j=0}^\infty \phi^j B^j Z_t = \sum_{j=0}^\infty \phi^j Z_{t-j} \tag{0.7}\] This proves that \((1 - \phi B)^{-1}\) obeys the exact geometric series formula \(\frac{1}{1 - r} = \sum_{j=0}^\infty r^j\) whenever \(|\phi| < 1\).


1.4.3 Sample Problem 0.3 (Lag Operator Algebra)
Statement: Rewrite \(X_t = 0.5 X_{t-1} + Z_t - 0.2 Z_{t-1}\) using \(B\), and expand \(X_t\) in terms of \(Z_t, Z_{t-1}, Z_{t-2}\).
Solution: 1. \((1 - 0.5 B) X_t = (1 - 0.2 B) Z_t\). 2. Inverting \((1 - 0.5 B)\): \[X_t = (1 + 0.5 B + 0.25 B^2 + \dots)(1 - 0.2 B) Z_t = \big[1 + (0.5 - 0.2)B + (0.25 - 0.10)B^2 + \dots\big] Z_t\] Hence \(X_t = Z_t + 0.30 Z_{t-1} + 0.15 Z_{t-2} + \dots\).






Key Takeaway: Section 0.4



The lag operator \(B\) turns messy subscript recursions into clean polynomial algebra. Whenever \(|\phi| < 1\), \((1 - \phi B)^{-1}\) expands into a decaying infinite sum of past shocks.

text:
1.5 Complex Numbers & The Unit Circle (Why Oscillations Happen)
When a second-order difference equation \(X_t - \phi_1 X_{t-1} - \phi_2 X_{t-2} = Z_t\) has a negative discriminant, its characteristic polynomial \(\Phi(z) = 1 - \phi_1 z - \phi_2 z^2 = 0\) produces complex conjugate roots. In time series, complex roots are not abstract—they are the mathematical signature of cycles (like \(10\text{ Hz}\) EEG alpha waves or business cycles) [1], [3].

1.5.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

Complex Number (\(z = a + bi\)): A point in the 2D complex plane with real part \(a\), imaginary part \(b\), modulus \(r = |z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\), and phase angle \(\theta = \mathrm{atan2}(b, a)\).
Euler’s Formula: \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\), linking complex exponentials directly to sinusoidal waves.
Unit Circle: The circle \(|z| = 1\) in the complex plane separating stable decaying processes (\(|z| > 1\)) from exploding processes (\(|z| < 1\)).



1.5.2 First-Principles Derivation: Root Modulus, Stability, and Oscillation Frequency
Suppose the characteristic polynomial \(\Phi(z) = 1 - \phi_1 z - \phi_2 z^2 = 0\) has complex conjugate roots \(z_1, z_2 = r e^{\pm i\theta}\). Because \(\Phi(z) = (1 - z/z_1)(1 - z/z_2)\): 1. Comparing coefficients of \(z^2\): \(\frac{1}{z_1 z_2} = -\phi_2 \implies \frac{1}{r^2} = -\phi_2 \implies r = |z_1| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{-\phi_2}}\). Thus, stability (\(|z| > 1\)) requires \(-\phi_2 < 1 \iff \phi_2 > -1\). 2. Comparing coefficients of \(z\): \(\frac{1}{z_1} + \frac{1}{z_2} = \phi_1 \implies \frac{2\cos\theta}{r} = \phi_1\). Substituting \(r = 1/\sqrt{-\phi_2}\): \[\cos\theta = \frac{\phi_1}{2\sqrt{-\phi_2}} \implies \theta = \arccos\left(\frac{\phi_1}{2\sqrt{-\phi_2}}\right) \tag{0.8}\] Since each discrete time step advances the phase by \(\theta\) radians, a full \(2\pi\) cycle takes \(T = \frac{2\pi}{\theta}\) samples. Given sampling rate \(f_s\) (Hz), the physical frequency is: \[f = \frac{f_s \, \theta}{2\pi}\text{ Hz} \tag{0.9}\]


1.5.3 Sample Problem 0.4 (Unit Circle Stability & Oscillation Period)
Statement: Find the roots of \(\Phi(z) = 1 - 1.2 z + 0.5 z^2 = 0\), verify whether \(|z| > 1\), and compute the oscillation period \(T\).
Solution: Solving \(0.5 z^2 - 1.2 z + 1 = 0\): \[z = \frac{1.2 \pm \sqrt{1.44 - 2.00}}{1.0} = 1.2 \pm 0.7483\,i\] Modulus: \(|z| = \sqrt{1.2^2 + 0.7483^2} = \sqrt{2.0} \approx 1.414 > 1\) (strictly outside the unit circle \(\implies\) stable). Angle: \(\theta = \arccos\left(\frac{1.2}{2\sqrt{0.5}}\right) = \arccos(0.8485) \approx 0.5576\text{ rad}\), giving period \(T = \frac{2\pi}{0.5576} \approx 11.27\text{ steps}\).






Key Takeaway: Section 0.5



The modulus \(|z|\) of characteristic roots governs stability (\(|z| > 1\) means shocks decay), while the angle \(\theta\) governs oscillation period (\(T = 2\pi/\theta\)).

section: 1.6 Financial Returns vs. Raw Prices (Essential Transformation)
text:
1.6 Financial Returns vs. Raw Prices (Essential Transformation)
Raw stock prices \(P_t\) drift upward over decades and have expanding variance, making them non-stationary [4]. Analysts therefore convert prices into returns.

1.6.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

Simple Return (\(R_t\)): \(R_t = \frac{P_t - P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}}\). Additive across assets in a portfolio, but not across time.
Log Return (\(r_t\)): \(r_t = \ln\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}\right) = \ln(P_t) - \ln(P_{t-1}) = \nabla \ln(P_t)\). Additive across time!



1.6.2 First-Principles Proof: Time-Additivity & Small-Return Equivalence
For a \(k\)-day horizon from \(t-k\) to \(t\): \[r_t + r_{t-1} + \dots + r_{t-k+1} = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} \big(\ln P_{t-j} - \ln P_{t-j-1}\big) = \ln P_t - \ln P_{t-k} = \ln\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-k}}\right) \tag{0.10}\] All intermediate prices telescope out! Moreover, since \(P_t / P_{t-1} = 1 + R_t\), a first-order Taylor expansion \(\ln(1 + R_t) = R_t - \frac{R_t^2}{2} + \dots\) shows \(r_t \approx R_t\) when \(|R_t| \ll 1\).


1.6.3 Sample Problem 0.5 (Simple vs. Log Returns)
Statement: A stock closes at \(P_0 = 100\), \(P_1 = 105\), \(P_2 = 99.75\). Compute \(R_1, R_2\) and \(r_1, r_2\), and verify time-additivity.
Solution: \(R_1 = +0.05\), \(R_2 = -0.05\), so \(R_1 + R_2 = 0\) (misleading, since \(P_2 < P_0\)). By contrast, \(r_1 = \ln(1.05) = +0.04879\), \(r_2 = \ln(0.95) = -0.05129\), and \(r_1 + r_2 = -0.00250 = \ln(99.75/100)\), matching the true \(-0.25\%\) cumulative drop.






Key Takeaway: Section 0.6



Always model log returns \(r_t = \nabla \ln(P_t)\) rather than raw price levels \(P_t\) when analyzing single-asset time series dynamics; log returns telescope cleanly across multi-day horizons.

1.8 Summary of Concepts (Chapter 0)

Time-Order Dependence: Unlike tabular \(i.i.d.\) data, temporal observations inherit past states; shuffling destroys causality and memory.

2.1 The Illusion of Independence and the Birth of Temporal Memory
In February 1926, George Udny Yule delivered a historic address before the Royal Statistical Society entitled “Why do we sometimes get nonsense-correlations between Time-Series?” Yule demonstrated that if you compute the ordinary Pearson correlation between two completely unrelated temporal sequences—such as the annual mortality rate in England and the proportion of Church of England marriages—you frequently obtain a correlation exceeding \(0.95\), with conventional \(t\)-tests screaming significance at \(p < 0.0001\).
Why did classical statistics fail so catastrophically? Because time possesses inertia. Observations close together in time inherit the state of their predecessors. One year later, in 1927, the Soviet economist Eugen Slutsky published an equally startling revelation: if you take a sequence of pure, uncorrelated lottery draws (white noise) and apply consecutive moving averages, the resulting series exhibits smooth, undulating waves that mimic economic cycles—or cortical brainwaves—with uncanny fidelity. Slutsky proved that apparent rhythms arise naturally whenever random shocks are filtered through linear memory over time [1].
Whether you are decoding EEG voltage fluctuations from a patient’s scalp or modeling daily equity returns for a quantitative portfolio, your first task is always the same: measure how fast the past fades, separate true signal dynamics from random noise, and verify whether the statistical rules governing the series stay constant over time [3], [4].

text:
2.2 Stochastic Processes and Basic Statistical Moments
To formalize time-ordered data, we model an observed time series not as a list of fixed numbers, but as one realization drawn from an underlying stochastic process [2].

2.2.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

Stochastic Process (\(\{X_t(\omega) : t \in \mathcal{T}\}\)): An indexed collection of random variables defined on a common probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})\). Here \(\mathcal{T} = \mathbb{Z}\) denotes discrete time ticks.
Sample Path / Realization (\(\{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N\}\)): A single observed trajectory corresponding to one outcome \(\omega_0 \in \Omega\) (e.g., one 5-second EEG recording or one historical S&P 500 path).
Mean Function (\(\mu_t\)): The expected value at time \(t\): \(\mu_t = \mathbb{E}[X_t]\).
Autocovariance Function (\(\gamma(s, t)\)): Measures the linear dependence between the process at time \(s\) and time \(t\): \[\gamma(s, t) = \mathrm{Cov}(X_s, X_t) = \mathbb{E}\big[(X_s - \mu_s)(X_t - \mu_t)\big] \tag{1.1}\]
Autocorrelation Function (\(\rho(s, t)\)): The scale-free correlation between \(X_s\) and \(X_t\): \[\rho(s, t) = \frac{\gamma(s, t)}{\sqrt{\gamma(s, s)\gamma(t, t)}} \in [-1, 1] \tag{1.2}\]



2.2.2 First-Principles Result: Cauchy-Schwarz Bound on \(\rho(s, t)\)
Theorem 1.1: For any two times \(s, t\), \(|\gamma(s, t)| \le \sqrt{\gamma(s, s)\gamma(t, t)}\), so \(|\rho(s, t)| \le 1\).
Derivation from First Principles: Let \(\tilde{X}_s = X_s - \mu_s\) and \(\tilde{X}_t = X_t - \mu_t\). For any real scalar \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\), the squared random variable \((\tilde{X}_s + \lambda \tilde{X}_t)^2 \ge 0\) has non-negative expectation: \[g(\lambda) = \mathbb{E}\big[(\tilde{X}_s + \lambda \tilde{X}_t)^2\big] = \gamma(t, t)\lambda^2 + 2\gamma(s, t)\lambda + \gamma(s, s) \ge 0 \tag{1.3}\] Because this quadratic in \(\lambda\) is never negative, its discriminant cannot be positive: \[4\gamma(s, t)^2 - 4\gamma(s, s)\gamma(t, t) \le 0 \implies \gamma(s, t)^2 \le \gamma(s, s)\gamma(t, t) \implies |\rho(s, t)| \le 1\]


2.2.3 Sample Problem 1.1 (Moments of a Random Walk)
Statement: Let \(X_t = \sum_{i=1}^t Z_i\) where \(Z_i \sim WN(0, \sigma^2)\) and \(t \ge 1\). Compute \(\mu_t\), \(\gamma(t, t)\), and \(\gamma(s, t)\) for \(s \le t\).
Solution:

\(\mu_t = \sum_{i=1}^t \mathbb{E}[Z_i] = 0\).
\(\gamma(t, t) = \mathrm{Var}(\sum_{i=1}^t Z_i) = \sum_{i=1}^t \mathrm{Var}(Z_i) = t\sigma^2\) (variance grows linearly with time!).
For \(s \le t\): \(\gamma(s, t) = \mathrm{Cov}(\sum_{i=1}^s Z_i, \sum_{j=1}^t Z_j) = \sum_{i=1}^s \mathrm{Var}(Z_i) = s\sigma^2 = \min(s, t)\sigma^2\).







Key Takeaway:



A stochastic process generalizes a single random variable to an infinite sequence of correlated variables. Notice in Problem 1.1 that a Random Walk’s variance \(t\sigma^2\) grows with \(t\), which means its rules are not time-invariant.

text:
2.3 Stationarity: Strict vs. Weak (Time-Invariance)
If the mean \(\mu_t\) and covariance \(\gamma(s, t)\) shifted arbitrarily at every tick, a single historical series of length \(N\) would never be enough to estimate them. Stationarity imposes time-invariance so historical patterns can generalize to the future [3].

2.3.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms






Definition 1.1: Strict Stationarity



A process \(\{X_t\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}\) is strictly stationary if all joint finite-dimensional distributions are invariant under arbitrary calendar shifts \(h \in \mathbb{Z}\): \[F_{t_1, \dots, t_k}(c_1, \dots, c_k) = F_{t_1+h, \dots, t_k+h}(c_1, \dots, c_k) \tag{1.4}\]








Definition 1.2: Weak (Second-Order) Stationarity



A process \(\{X_t\}_{t \in \mathbb{Z}}\) is weakly stationary (covariance stationary) if:

\(\mathbb{E}[X_t^2] < \infty\) for all \(t \in \mathbb{Z}\),
\(\mathbb{E}[X_t] = \mu\) (constant across all \(t\)), and
\(\mathrm{Cov}(X_t, X_{t+h}) = \gamma(h)\) depends only on the lag separation \(h\), not on \(t\).



For weakly stationary processes, we write the ACF with a single lag argument \(h\): \[\rho(h) = \frac{\gamma(h)}{\gamma(0)} \tag{1.5}\]


2.3.2 First-Principles Properties of \(\gamma(h)\)
Theorem 1.2: A weakly stationary ACVF \(\gamma(h)\) satisfies:

\(\gamma(0) = \mathrm{Var}(X_t) \ge 0\),
\(\gamma(h) = \gamma(-h)\) (even symmetry), and
Positive Semi-Definiteness: For any \(n \ge 1\) and constants \(a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_i a_j \gamma(t_i - t_j) \ge 0\).

Derivation from First Principles: Symmetry follows directly from \(\gamma(h) = \mathrm{Cov}(X_t, X_{t+h}) = \mathrm{Cov}(X_{t+h}, X_t) = \gamma(-h)\) (setting \(s = t+h\)). For positive semi-definiteness, define the linear combination \(W = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_{t_i}\). Since variance is non-negative and covariance is bilinear: \[0 \le \mathrm{Var}(W) = \mathrm{Cov}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_{t_i}, \sum_{j=1}^n a_j X_{t_j}\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_i a_j \gamma(t_i - t_j) \tag{1.6}\]


2.3.3 Sample Problem 1.2 (Testing Weak Stationarity)
Statement: Let \(Z_t \sim WN(0, \sigma^2)\). Test whether \(Y_t = 0.3 t + Z_t\) and \(W_t = (-1)^t Z_t\) are weakly stationary.
Solution:

For \(Y_t\): \(\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = 0.3 t\) depends on \(t\) \(\implies\) Non-stationary.
For \(W_t\): \(\mathbb{E}[W_t] = (-1)^t \cdot 0 = 0\) (constant). Covariance: \(\mathrm{Cov}(W_t, W_{t+h}) = (-1)^{2t+h}\mathrm{Cov}(Z_t, Z_{t+h})\), which equals \(\sigma^2\) if \(h=0\) and \(0\) if \(h \neq 0\). Since both moments are independent of \(t\), \(W_t\) is weakly stationary.







Key Takeaway:



Weak stationarity requires three things: finite variance, constant mean, and lag-only autocovariance. For Gaussian processes, weak stationarity automatically implies strict stationarity [2].

section: 2.4 Ergodicity: Bridging Ensemble Space and Historical Time
text:
2.4 Ergodicity: Bridging Ensemble Space and Historical Time
In clinical trials, we average across 500 patients. In EEG or financial analysis, we observe one continuous historical trajectory \(\{x_1, \dots, x_N\}\). Ergodicity tells us when a time average \(\bar{X}_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^N X_t\) converges to the ensemble expectation \(\mu\) [1].

2.4.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

Sample Mean (\(\bar{X}_N\)): \(\bar{X}_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^N X_t\).
Ergodic for the Mean: A weakly stationary process is ergodic for the mean if \(\lim_{N\to\infty} \mathbb{E}[(\bar{X}_N - \mu)^2] = 0\) (mean-square convergence).



2.4.2 First-Principles Derivation: Ergodicity of the Mean
Theorem 1.3: A weakly stationary process \(\{X_t\}\) with autocovariance \(\gamma(h)\) is ergodic for the mean if and only if \(\lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{h=0}^{N-1}\gamma(h) = 0\). A sufficient condition is \(\sum_{h=0}^\infty |\gamma(h)| < \infty\).
Derivation from First Principles: First, \(\mathbb{E}[\bar{X}_N] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^N \mu = \mu\), so \(\mathbb{E}[(\bar{X}_N - \mu)^2] = \mathrm{Var}(\bar{X}_N)\). Applying bilinearity of covariance: \[\mathrm{Var}(\bar{X}_N) = \frac{1}{N^2} \sum_{s=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^N \mathrm{Cov}(X_s, X_t) = \frac{1}{N^2} \sum_{s=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^N \gamma(s - t) \tag{1.7}\] Group pairs \((s, t)\) by their lag \(h = s - t \in \{-(N-1), \dots, N-1\}\). For each fixed \(h\), there are exactly \(N - |h|\) pairs satisfying \(s - t = h\). Using \(\gamma(h) = \gamma(-h)\): \[\mathrm{Var}(\bar{X}_N) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{h=-(N-1)}^{N-1} \left(1 - \frac{|h|}{N}\right)\gamma(h) = \frac{\gamma(0)}{N} + \frac{2}{N}\sum_{h=1}^{N-1}\left(1 - \frac{h}{N}\right)\gamma(h) \tag{1.8}\] If \(\sum_{h=0}^\infty |\gamma(h)| < \infty\), then \(|\mathrm{Var}(\bar{X}_N)| \le \frac{1}{N}\sum_{h=-\infty}^\infty |\gamma(h)| \to 0\) as \(N \to \infty\).


2.4.3 Sample Problem 1.3 (Multi-Period Variance Inflation)
Statement: Daily portfolio returns follow \(r_t\) with \(\gamma(0) = 0.0001\) and \(\gamma(1) = 0.000025\) (\(\gamma(h)=0\) for \(h \ge 2\)). Compute \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar{r}_2)\) using Eq. (1.8) and compare with the naive \(i.i.d.\) formula \(\gamma(0)/2\).
Solution: By Eq. (1.8) with \(N = 2\): \[\mathrm{Var}(\bar{r}_2) = \frac{\gamma(0)}{2} + \frac{2}{2}\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}\right)\gamma(1) = \frac{0.0001}{2} + 0.5(0.000025) = 0.00005 + 0.0000125 = 0.0000625\] The naive \(i.i.d.\) formula gives \(0.00005\), underestimating variance by \(25\%\)!






Key Takeaway:



Ergodicity holds when memory decays fast enough (\(\sum |\gamma(h)| < \infty\)) so distant time blocks act nearly independently. Moreover, Equation (1.8) warns us that positive autocorrelation inflates the variance of averages and multi-day portfolio returns.

section: 2.5 Sample ACF, Bartlett’s Bounds, and PACF
text:
2.5 Sample ACF, Bartlett’s Bounds, and PACF
In practice, we never observe \(\gamma(h)\) directly; we estimate it from a finite sample \(\{x_1, \dots, x_N\}\) [2], [3].

2.5.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

Sample ACVF (\(\hat{\gamma}(h)\)): \(\hat{\gamma}(h) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N-h} (x_t - \bar{x})(x_{t+h} - \bar{x})\). (Dividing by \(N\) ensures the sample covariance matrix remains positive semi-definite.)
Sample ACF (\(\hat{\rho}(h)\)): \(\hat{\rho}(h) = \frac{\hat{\gamma}(h)}{\hat{\gamma}(0)}\).
Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF, \(\phi_{hh}\)): The direct correlation between \(X_t\) and \(X_{t-h}\) after linearly projecting out the intermediate variables \(\{X_{t-1}, \dots, X_{t-h+1}\}\): \[\phi_{hh} = \mathrm{Corr}\Big(X_t - \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_1^{h-1}} X_t, \; X_{t-h} - \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_1^{h-1}} X_{t-h}\Big) \tag{1.9}\]



2.5.2 First-Principles Results: Bartlett’s Bounds & Yule-Walker System

Bartlett’s White Noise Asymptotic Variance: For \(Z_t \sim WN(0, \sigma^2)\) and large \(N\), \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\rho}(h)) \approx \frac{1}{N}\) for all \(h \ge 1\) [2]. This gives the 95% white noise band: \[\pm \frac{1.96}{\sqrt{N}} \tag{1.10}\]
Yule-Walker Derivation: Regress \(X_t = \phi_{h1} X_{t-1} + \dots + \phi_{hh} X_{t-h} + \epsilon_t\), where \(\epsilon_t\) is orthogonal to \(X_{t-1}, \dots, X_{t-h}\). Multiplying both sides by \(X_{t-k}\) (\(k = 1, \dots, h\)), taking expectations, and dividing by \(\gamma(0)\) yields: \[\rho(k) = \sum_{j=1}^h \phi_{hj} \rho(k - j), \quad k = 1, \dots, h \tag{1.11}\] In matrix form, \(\mathbf{R}_h \boldsymbol{\phi}_h = \boldsymbol{\rho}_h\), whose final entry \(\phi_{hh}\) is the PACF at lag \(h\).
Durbin-Levinson Recursion: Solves Eq. (1.11) in \(\mathcal{O}(h^2)\) operations starting from \(\phi_{11} = \rho(1)\): \[\phi_{hh} = \frac{\rho(h) - \sum_{j=1}^{h-1} \phi_{h-1,j}\rho(h-j)}{1 - \sum_{j=1}^{h-1} \phi_{h-1,j}\rho(j)}, \qquad \phi_{hj} = \phi_{h-1,j} - \phi_{hh}\phi_{h-1,h-j} \tag{1.12}\]



2.5.3 Sample Problem 1.4 (Manual Sample ACF & Bartlett Test)
Statement: For the 5-point demeaned series \(x = \{2, 1, -1, -2, 0\}\), compute \(\hat{\gamma}(0)\), \(\hat{\gamma}(1)\), and \(\hat{\rho}(1)\) by hand.
Solution: \(\bar{x} = 0\). \(\hat{\gamma}(0) = \frac{1}{5}(4 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 0) = 2.0\). \(\hat{\gamma}(1) = \frac{1}{5}[(2)(1) + (1)(-1) + (-1)(-2) + (-2)(0)] = \frac{3}{5} = 0.6\). Hence \(\hat{\rho}(1) = \frac{0.6}{2.0} = 0.30\).






Key Takeaway:



The ACF measures total correlation (direct + indirect), whereas the PACF isolates direct lag-\(h\) dependence. Bartlett’s \(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{N}\) bands tell us whether sample spikes are statistically distinguishable from pure white noise.

text:
2.6 Wold Decomposition and Linear Processes

2.6.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

General Linear Process: \(X_t = \mu + \sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_j Z_{t-j}\) with \(\sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_j^2 < \infty\).
Purely Indeterministic vs. Deterministic: A process is purely indeterministic if its distant past carries zero predictive power (\(\lim_{m\to\infty}\mathrm{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X_t|\mathcal{M}_{-\infty}^{t-m}]) = 0\)).



2.6.2 Theorem 1.4: Wold Decomposition Theorem (1938)
Any zero-mean weakly stationary process \(\{X_t\}\) admits a unique orthogonal decomposition [1], [3]: \[X_t = \sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_j Z_{t-j} + V_t, \quad \psi_0 = 1, \quad \sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_j^2 < \infty \tag{1.13}\] where \(Z_t = X_t - \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{-\infty}^{t-1}} X_t \sim WN(0, \sigma^2)\) is the one-step innovation, \(V_t\) is deterministic (\(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{-\infty}^{t-1}} V_t = V_t\)), and \(\mathrm{Cov}(Z_s, V_t) = 0\) for all \(s, t\).






Key Takeaway:



Wold’s theorem guarantees that every regular stationary time series—from EEG rhythms to stationary asset returns—can be represented as a linear filter of white noise shocks.

text:
2.7 Autoregressive Models: AR(\(p\))
An AR(\(p\)) process models \(X_t\) as a linear combination of its past \(p\) values plus a fresh shock \(Z_t \sim WN(0, \sigma^2)\) [3]: \[X_t = \phi_1 X_{t-1} + \dots + \phi_p X_{t-p} + Z_t \iff \Phi(B) X_t = Z_t \tag{1.14}\] where \(\Phi(B) = 1 - \phi_1 B - \dots - \phi_p B^p\) is the autoregressive characteristic polynomial.

2.7.1 First-Principles Derivation: Moments, ACF, and PACF of AR(1)
Consider \(X_t = \phi X_{t-1} + Z_t\) with \(|\phi| < 1\). From Chapter 0 (Eq. 0.7), \(X_t = \sum_{j=0}^\infty \phi^j Z_{t-j}\). 1. Mean: \(\mathbb{E}[X_t] = \sum_{j=0}^\infty \phi^j \mathbb{E}[Z_{t-j}] = 0\). 2. Variance: Since \(Z_{t-j}\) are uncorrelated, \[\gamma(0) = \mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_{j=0}^\infty \phi^j Z_{t-j}\right) = \sum_{j=0}^\infty \phi^{2j}\sigma^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{1 - \phi^2} \tag{1.15}\] 3. ACF: Multiply \(X_t = \phi X_{t-1} + Z_t\) by \(X_{t-h}\) (\(h \ge 1\)) and take expectations. Since \(Z_t\) is uncorrelated with \(X_{t-h}\): \[\gamma(h) = \phi\gamma(h-1) \implies \gamma(h) = \phi^h \gamma(0) \implies \rho(h) = \phi^h \tag{1.16}\] 4. PACF: By Eq. (1.11), \(\phi_{11} = \rho(1) = \phi\). For \(h = 2\), \(\phi_{22} = \frac{\rho(2) - \rho(1)^2}{1 - \rho(1)^2} = \frac{\phi^2 - \phi^2}{1 - \phi^2} = 0\). By induction, \(\phi_{hh} = 0\) for all \(h \ge 2\).


2.7.2 Theorem 1.5: Causality Condition for AR(\(p\))
An AR(\(p\)) process \(\Phi(B)X_t = Z_t\) is causal (\(X_t = \sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_j Z_{t-j}\) with \(\sum |\psi_j| < \infty\)) if and only if all roots of \(\Phi(z) = 0\) lie strictly outside the unit circle (\(|z| > 1\)) [1], [3].


2.7.3 Sample Problem 1.5 (AR(2) Causality & Yule-Walker)
Statement: For \(X_t = 0.7 X_{t-1} - 0.1 X_{t-2} + Z_t\) (\(\sigma^2 = 1.44\)), verify causality and find \(\rho(1), \rho(2), \gamma(0)\).
Solution: \(\Phi(z) = 1 - 0.7z + 0.1z^2 = (1 - 0.5z)(1 - 0.2z) = 0 \implies z_1 = 2, z_2 = 5\) (both \(|z_i| > 1\), causal). Yule-Walker: \(\rho(1) = 0.7 - 0.1\rho(1) \implies \rho(1) = 0.7/1.1 \approx 0.6364\); \(\rho(2) = 0.7(0.6364) - 0.1 \approx 0.3455\). Variance: \(\gamma(0)[1 - 0.7\rho(1) + 0.1\rho(2)] = 1.44 \implies \gamma(0) \approx 2.4448\).






Key Takeaway:



An AR(\(p\)) process has infinite shock memory: its ACF tails off (exponentially or as a damped sine wave), while its PACF cuts off sharply after lag \(p\).

text:
2.8 Moving Average Models: MA(\(q\))
An MA(\(q\)) process expresses \(X_t\) as a finite linear combination of current and past white noise shocks [3]: \[X_t = Z_t + \theta_1 Z_{t-1} + \dots + \theta_q Z_{t-q} = \Theta(B) Z_t \tag{1.17}\]

2.8.1 First-Principles Derivation: Moments & Invertibility of MA(1)
Consider \(X_t = Z_t + \theta Z_{t-1}\) with \(Z_t \sim WN(0, \sigma^2)\). 1. Mean & Variance: \(\mathbb{E}[X_t] = 0\), and \(\gamma(0) = \mathrm{Var}(Z_t) + \theta^2\mathrm{Var}(Z_{t-1}) = \sigma^2(1 + \theta^2)\). 2. Autocovariance & ACF: \[\gamma(1) = \mathbb{E}[(Z_t + \theta Z_{t-1})(Z_{t-1} + \theta Z_{t-2})] = \theta \sigma^2, \qquad \gamma(h) = 0 \quad (|h| \ge 2) \tag{1.18}\] \[\rho(1) = \frac{\theta}{1 + \theta^2} \in [-0.5, 0.5], \qquad \rho(h) = 0 \quad (|h| \ge 2) \tag{1.19}\] 3. Invertibility: Notice that \(\theta\) and \(1/\theta\) yield the exact same \(\rho(1)\). To uniquely recover shocks \(Z_t\) from observed data via \(Z_t = (1 + \theta B)^{-1} X_t = \sum_{j=0}^\infty (-\theta)^j X_{t-j}\) with decaying weights, we require \(|\theta| < 1\). In general, an MA(\(q\)) model is invertible if and only if all roots of \(\Theta(z) = 0\) satisfy \(|z| > 1\) [2].


2.8.2 Sample Problem 1.6 (MA(1) Identifiability)
Statement: Compare Model A (\(X_t = Z_t + 2.5 Z_{t-1}\), \(\sigma_Z^2 = 0.16\)) and Model B (\(\tilde{X}_t = E_t + 0.4 E_{t-1}\), \(\sigma_E^2 = 1.00\)).
Solution: Both yield \(\gamma(0) = 1.16\), \(\gamma(1) = 0.40\), and \(\gamma(h) = 0\) (\(|h|\ge 2\)). However, Model A has root \(z = -0.4\) (\(|z| < 1\), non-invertible), while Model B has root \(z = -2.5\) (\(|z| > 1\), invertible). Only Model B is valid for forecasting.






Key Takeaway:



An MA(\(q\)) process has finite shock memory: its ACF cuts off sharply after lag \(q\), while its PACF tails off. Always select the invertible representation (\(|z| > 1\)).

2.9 3-Tier Graduated Problem Ladder (Beginner to Domain Mastery)

2.9.1 Tier 1: By-Hand Intuition

Problem 1.7 (Practice): Compute \(\bar{x}\), \(\hat{\gamma}(0)\), \(\hat{\gamma}(1)\), and \(\hat{\rho}(1)\) by hand for \(x = \{4, 2, 0, -2, -4\}\). (Answer: \(\bar{x}=0\), \(\hat{\gamma}(0)=8.0\), \(\hat{\gamma}(1)=4.0\), \(\hat{\rho}(1)=0.50\).)
Problem 1.8 (Practice): For \(X_t = Z_t - 0.6 Z_{t-1}\) with \(Z_t \sim WN(0, 2.5)\), compute \(\gamma(0)\), \(\gamma(1)\), \(\rho(1)\), \(\rho(2)\), and verify invertibility. (Answer: \(\gamma(0)=3.4\), \(\gamma(1)=-1.5\), \(\rho(1)\approx -0.441\), \(\rho(2)=0\); invertible since \(|z|=1.67 > 1\).)



2.9.2 Tier 2: Analytical & Exam-Style

Problem 1.9 (Worked — Signal-Plus-Noise Durbin-Levinson): An EEG electrode records \(X_t = S_t + V_t\), where \(S_t = 0.8 S_{t-1} + W_t\) (\(\sigma_W^2 = 0.36\)) and independent sensor noise \(V_t \sim WN(0, 0.64)\). Compute \(\rho_X(1), \rho_X(2)\), and \(\phi_{22}\). Solution: \(\gamma_S(0) = \frac{0.36}{1 - 0.64} = 1.00\), so \(\gamma_X(0) = 1.00 + 0.64 = 1.64\), while \(\gamma_X(h) = \gamma_S(h) = 0.8^h\) for \(h \ge 1\). Thus \(\rho_X(1) = \frac{0.80}{1.64} \approx 0.4878\) and \(\rho_X(2) = \frac{0.64}{1.64} \approx 0.3902\). By Eq. (1.12): \[\phi_{22} = \frac{0.3902 - (0.4878)^2}{1 - (0.4878)^2} = \frac{0.1522}{0.7620} \approx 0.1997 \neq 0\] Adding measurement noise turns a pure AR(1) into an ARMA(1,1) whose PACF no longer cuts off at lag 1.



2.9.3 Tier 3: Domain Case Studies (EEG Signals & Financial Analytics)

2.9.3.1 Problem 1.10: EEG Alpha-Wave Resonance via AR(2) Complex Roots (Biomedical — Worked)
Statement: A resting-state EEG segment sampled at \(f_s = 100\text{ Hz}\) follows \(X_t = 1.458 X_{t-1} - 0.810 X_{t-2} + Z_t\). Verify stationarity and compute the dominant frequency in Hz.
Solution:

Characteristic polynomial: \(\Phi(z) = 1 - 1.458z + 0.810z^2 = 0\). Here \(\phi_1 = 1.458, \phi_2 = -0.810\).
Root modulus (Section 0.5): \(|z| = 1/\sqrt{-\phi_2} = 1/\sqrt{0.810} = 1/0.9 \approx 1.111 > 1\) (stationary).
Frequency (Eq. 0.8–0.9): \(\cos\theta = \frac{1.458}{2\sqrt{0.810}} = 0.810 \implies \theta \approx 0.6266\text{ rad}\), so \(f = \frac{100 \times 0.6266}{2\pi} \approx 9.97\text{ Hz}\) (classic \(10\text{ Hz}\) alpha rhythm!).



2.9.3.2 Problem 1.11: Testing Weak-Form Market Efficiency with Bartlett Bounds (Finance — Worked)
Statement: An analyst observes sample ACF values \(\hat{\rho}(1) = 0.095\), \(\hat{\rho}(2) = -0.040\), \(\hat{\rho}(3) = 0.025\) from \(N = 625\) daily log returns. Test against white noise at the 5% level.
Solution: Bartlett’s 95% bound (Eq. 1.10) is \(\pm \frac{1.96}{\sqrt{625}} = \pm 0.0784\). Because \(|\hat{\rho}(1)| = 0.095 > 0.0784\), lag-1 autocorrelation is statistically significant, rejecting pure white noise at lag 1.


2.9.3.3 Problem 1.12: Portfolio Variance Inflation (Practice)
Statement: Daily fund returns follow \(r_t = 0.25 r_{t-1} + Z_t\) with \(\gamma(0) = 0.0001\). Compute \(\mathrm{Var}(r_1 + r_2)\) and compare with \(2\gamma(0)\). (Answer: \(0.00025\) vs. naive \(0.00020\) — 25% higher.)

2.10 Dual-Track Laboratory Experimental Section






Dual-Track Lab Objectives (CO1 Focus)




Track A (Biomedical / EEG Signal Analysis): Check epoch stationarity, plot sample ACF/PACF, fit AR(\(p\)), and extract the dominant neural oscillation frequency from characteristic roots.
Track B (Financial & Portfolio Analytics): Transform asset levels into log returns, test predictability via Bartlett’s 95% bounds, compute autocorrelation-adjusted portfolio variance, and benchmark AR(1) against a random-walk mean.




2.10.1 Lab Track A: EEG Signal Spectral & AR(\(p\)) Modeling
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.tsa.ar_model import AutoReg

fs = 100  # 100 Hz sampling rate
t = np.arange(0, 5.0, 1/fs)
np.random.seed(42)

# Resting-state eyes-closed EEG (10 Hz alpha + 22 Hz beta + colored noise)
alpha_wave = 15.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10.0 * t + 0.3)
beta_wave  =  4.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 22.0 * t)
bg_noise = np.zeros(len(t))
eps = np.random.normal(0, 3.5, len(t))
for i in range(1, len(t)):
    bg_noise[i] = 0.7 * bg_noise[i-1] + eps[i]

eeg_series = pd.Series(alpha_wave + beta_wave + bg_noise, index=pd.Index(t, name="Time (s)"))

mid = len(eeg_series) // 2
print("--- Track A: EEG Epoch Stationarity Check ---")
print(f"First Half  -> Mean: {eeg_series.iloc[:mid].mean():.2f} uV, Std: {eeg_series.iloc[:mid].std():.2f} uV")
print(f"Second Half -> Mean: {eeg_series.iloc[mid:].mean():.2f} uV, Std: {eeg_series.iloc[mid:].std():.2f} uV")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(11, 9))
axes[0].plot(eeg_series.index, eeg_series.values, color="#0f766e", lw=1.1)
axes[0].set_title("Resting-State EEG Trace (100 Hz Sampling)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Amplitude (uV)")
axes[0].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

sm.graphics.tsa.plot_acf(eeg_series, lags=40, ax=axes[1], title="EEG Sample ACF")
sm.graphics.tsa.plot_pacf(eeg_series, lags=40, ax=axes[2], method="yule_walker", title="EEG Sample PACF")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

ar2_eeg = AutoReg(eeg_series.values, lags=2, old_names=False).fit()
phi1, phi2 = ar2_eeg.params[1], ar2_eeg.params[2]
roots = np.roots([-phi2, -phi1, 1.0])
print(f"\nAR(2): phi1={phi1:.4f}, phi2={phi2:.4f} | Root Moduli: {np.abs(roots)}")
if np.iscomplexobj(roots):
    dom_freq = fs * np.abs(np.angle(roots[0])) / (2 * np.pi)
    print(f"Extracted Dominant EEG Frequency: {dom_freq:.2f} Hz")


2.10.2 Lab Track B: Financial Return Stationarity & Portfolio Risk Scaling
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.tsa.ar_model import AutoReg
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf

macro = sm.datasets.macrodata.load_pandas().data
price_level = pd.Series(macro["realgdp"].values,
                        index=pd.period_range("1959Q1", periods=len(macro), freq="Q").to_timestamp())
log_returns = np.log(price_level / price_level.shift(1)).dropna()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 7))
axes[0, 0].plot(price_level, color="#1e3a8a")
axes[0, 0].set_title("Raw Index Level (Non-Stationary)")
axes[0, 1].plot(log_returns, color="#c2410c")
axes[0, 1].axhline(log_returns.mean(), color="black", ls="--", lw=0.8)
axes[0, 1].set_title("Log Returns (Approximately Stationary)")
sm.graphics.tsa.plot_acf(price_level, lags=20, ax=axes[1, 0], title="ACF of Raw Level")
sm.graphics.tsa.plot_acf(log_returns, lags=20, ax=axes[1, 1], title="ACF of Log Returns (Bartlett Bounds)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

acf_vals = acf(log_returns, nlags=5)
K = 4
naive_var = K * log_returns.var()
corr_factor = 1 + 2 * sum((1 - h / K) * acf_vals[h] for h in range(1, K))
print(f"Lag-1 ACF: {acf_vals[1]:.4f} | Portfolio Variance Inflation Factor (K={K}): {corr_factor:.3f}x")

split = int(len(log_returns) * 0.8)
train_r, test_r = log_returns.iloc[:split], log_returns.iloc[split:]
ar1_fin = AutoReg(train_r.values, lags=1, old_names=False).fit()
pred_ar1 = ar1_fin.predict(start=len(train_r), end=len(log_returns) - 1)
pred_naive = np.repeat(train_r.mean(), len(test_r))
print(f"Out-of-Sample RMSE -> AR(1): {np.sqrt(np.mean((test_r.values - pred_ar1)**2)):.5f} | Mean Baseline: {np.sqrt(np.mean((test_r.values - pred_naive)**2)):.5f}")

2.11 Summary of Concepts

Stationarity: Weak stationarity requires finite variance, constant mean, and lag-only autocovariance \(\gamma(h)\). It ensures historical patterns generalize across time.
Ergodicity: Guarantees that time averages (\(\bar{X}_N\)) converge to ensemble expectations (\(\mu\)) when \(\sum |\gamma(h)| < \infty\), and exposes how positive autocorrelation inflates multi-period portfolio risk.
ACF vs. PACF: ACF measures total linear dependence and cuts off after lag \(q\) for MA(\(q\)); PACF removes intermediate lags via Yule-Walker/Durbin-Levinson and cuts off after lag \(p\) for AR(\(p\)).
Wold Decomposition: Every regular stationary process is an infinite linear filter of white noise shocks.
Causality & Invertibility: Both require all roots of \(\Phi(z)=0\) (for AR) and \(\Theta(z)=0\) (for MA) to lie strictly outside the unit circle (\(|z| > 1\)).

text:
3.1 The Box-Jenkins Revolution and Volatility Clusters
In 1970, George Box and Gwilym Jenkins transformed forecasting from ad-hoc smoothing heuristics into a disciplined three-stage scientific loop: Identification \(\to\) Estimation \(\to\) Diagnostic Checking [3]. By combining difference operators \(\nabla^d = (1-B)^d\) with mixed ARMA polynomials, their ARIMA framework could tame drifting economic indices, industrial sensors, and seasonal demand with just a handful of parameters.
Yet even as ARIMA conquered mean forecasting, a blind spot remained: constant variance (homoscedasticity). In financial markets, daily stock returns are nearly uncorrelated in their direction (\(\rho(h) \approx 0\)), yet large price swings—positive or negative—arrive in tight clusters, followed by calm stretches. In 1982, Robert Engle solved this puzzle by letting the conditional variance \(\sigma_t^2\) evolve autoregressively as a function of past squared shocks (ARCH) [5], and Tim Bollerslev (1986) generalized it into GARCH [6]—forming the backbone of modern Value-at-Risk and portfolio risk management.

text:
3.2 Mixed ARMA(\(p,q\)) Models
When a pure AR(\(p\)) or pure MA(\(q\)) model requires too many parameters to capture both persistent feedback and finite shock memory, combining them yields a parsimonious ARMA(\(p,q\)) model [1], [3].

3.2.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms






Definition 2.1: ARMA(\(p,q\)) Process



A weakly stationary process \(\{X_t\}\) is ARMA(\(p,q\)) if it satisfies: \[\Phi(B) X_t = \Theta(B) Z_t, \qquad Z_t \sim WN(0, \sigma^2) \tag{2.1}\] where \(\Phi(B) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^p \phi_i B^i\) and \(\Theta(B) = 1 + \sum_{j=1}^q \theta_j B^j\).



Parameter Redundancy: When \(\Phi(z)\) and \(\Theta(z)\) share a common factor \((1 - c z)\), that factor cancels out, leaving a lower-order model with non-identifiable parameters.
Causality & Invertibility: Requires no common roots between \(\Phi(z)\) and \(\Theta(z)\), and all roots of both polynomials to lie strictly outside the unit circle (\(|z| > 1\)).



3.2.2 First-Principles Derivation: \(\psi\)-Weights of ARMA(1,1)
Consider \((1 - \phi B) X_t = (1 + \theta B) Z_t\) with \(|\phi| < 1\). Writing \(X_t = \Psi(B) Z_t = \sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_j Z_{t-j}\), we equate coefficients in \(\Phi(B)\Psi(B) = \Theta(B)\): \[(1 - \phi B)(\psi_0 + \psi_1 B + \psi_2 B^2 + \dots) = 1 + \theta B \tag{2.2}\]

\(B^0\): \(\psi_0 = 1\).
\(B^1\): \(\psi_1 - \phi\psi_0 = \theta \implies \psi_1 = \phi + \theta\).
\(B^j\) (\(j \ge 2\)): \(\psi_j - \phi\psi_{j-1} = 0 \implies \psi_j = \phi^{j-1}(\phi + \theta)\).



3.2.3 Sample Problem 2.1 (ARMA(1,1) \(\psi\)-Weights & Variance)
Statement: For \(X_t - 0.4 X_{t-1} = Z_t + 0.8 Z_{t-1}\) with \(Z_t \sim WN(0, 2.0)\), verify causality/invertibility, find \(\psi_0, \psi_1, \psi_2\), and compute \(\gamma(0)\).
Solution: Roots: \(z_\Phi = 2.5\) and \(z_\Theta = -1.25\) (both \(|z| > 1\), no common root \(\implies\) causal & invertible). \(\psi_0 = 1\), \(\psi_1 = 0.4 + 0.8 = 1.2\), \(\psi_2 = 0.4(1.2) = 0.48\). Using \(\gamma(0) = \sigma^2 \sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_j^2\): \[\gamma(0) = 2.0 \left(1 + \frac{(1.2)^2}{1 - 0.4^2}\right) = 2.0 \left(1 + \frac{1.44}{0.84}\right) = 2.0(1 + 1.7143) \approx 5.4286\]






Key Takeaway:



ARMA(\(p,q\)) models achieve parsimony by blending AR feedback and MA shock memory. Always check that \(\Phi(z)\) and \(\Theta(z)\) share no common roots before estimation.

text:
3.3 Non-Stationarity, Differencing, and ARIMA / SARIMA
Most raw asset prices, EEG baseline drifts, and macroeconomic series wander without a fixed mean. Differencing removes stochastic trends [2], [3].

3.3.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

Deterministic Trend: \(X_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + Y_t\) (stationary fluctuations around a fixed line; shocks are temporary).
Stochastic Trend (Unit Root): \(X_t = c + X_{t-1} + Z_t\) (shocks accumulate permanently; \(\mathrm{Var}(X_t | X_0) = t\sigma^2\)).
ARIMA(\(p,d,q\)): \(\Phi(B)(1 - B)^d X_t = \Theta(B) Z_t\), meaning \(W_t = \nabla^d X_t\) is a stationary ARMA(\(p,q\)) process.
Seasonal ARIMA (\(\mathrm{SARIMA}(p,d,q)\times(P,D,Q)_s\)): \[\Phi_p(B)\tilde{\Phi}_P(B^s)\nabla^d \nabla_s^D X_t = \Theta_q(B)\tilde{\Theta}_Q(B^s) Z_t \tag{2.3}\] where \(\nabla_s X_t = (1 - B^s) X_t = X_t - X_{t-s}\) removes repeating cycles of period \(s\).



3.3.2 First-Principles Result: The Hazard of Over-Differencing
Suppose \(X_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + Z_t\) is already trend-stationary. Applying \(\nabla = 1 - B\) gives: \[\nabla X_t = \beta_1 + Z_t - Z_{t-1} = \beta_1 + (1 - B)Z_t \tag{2.4}\] Differencing turned pure white noise into a non-invertible MA(1) process with \(\theta = -1\) (root \(z = 1\) on the unit circle) and doubled the innovation variance from \(\sigma^2\) to \(2\sigma^2\).


3.3.3 Sample Problem 2.2 (Expanding the Box-Jenkins Airline Model)
Statement: Expand the canonical \(\mathrm{SARIMA}(0,1,1)\times(0,1,1)_{12}\) equation \((1-B)(1-B^{12})X_t = (1 + \theta B)(1 + \tilde{\Theta} B^{12})Z_t\) into a one-step forecast formula for \(\hat{X}_{t+1|t}\).
Solution: Expanding LHS: \(X_t - X_{t-1} - X_{t-12} + X_{t-13}\). Expanding RHS: \(Z_t + \theta Z_{t-1} + \tilde{\Theta} Z_{t-12} + \theta\tilde{\Theta} Z_{t-13}\). Shifting \(t \to t+1\) and taking \(\mathbb{E}[\cdot | \mathcal{F}_t]\) (noting \(\mathbb{E}[Z_{t+1}|\mathcal{F}_t] = 0\)): \[\hat{X}_{t+1|t} = X_t + X_{t-11} - X_{t-12} + \theta \hat{z}_t + \tilde{\Theta} \hat{z}_{t-11} + \theta\tilde{\Theta} \hat{z}_{t-12}\]






Key Takeaway:



Use differencing (\(\nabla^d, \nabla_s^D\)) to eliminate stochastic unit roots and seasonal cycles, but stop as soon as stationarity is achieved to avoid injecting artificial unit-root MA(\(-1\)) terms.

text:
3.4 Multivariate Systems: Vector Autoregression (VAR(\(p\)))
In both multi-channel EEG (frontal, parietal, occipital electrodes) and multi-asset portfolios (equities, bonds, FX), variables co-evolve and lead or lag one another [2], [4].

3.4.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms






Definition 2.2: Vector Autoregressive Model VAR(\(p\))



Let \(\mathbf{Y}_t \in \mathbb{R}^K\). A \(\mathrm{VAR}(p)\) process satisfies: \[\mathbf{Y}_t = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{\Phi}_1 \mathbf{Y}_{t-1} + \dots + \mathbf{\Phi}_p \mathbf{Y}_{t-p} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t^T] = \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \tag{2.5}\]



Granger Causality: \(Y_j\) Granger-causes \(Y_i\) if past lags of \(Y_j\) improve forecasts of \(Y_{i,t}\) beyond \(Y_i\)’s own past (tested via joint Wald \(F\)-test on \(\Phi_{1,ij} = \dots = \Phi_{p,ij} = 0\)).
Impulse Response Function (IRF): Traces how a 1-unit orthogonalized shock in variable \(j\) propagates through all \(K\) variables over future steps \(h = 0, 1, 2, \dots\).



3.4.2 First-Principles Result: Companion Matrix Stability Condition
Any VAR(\(p\)) can be stacked into a \(Kp\)-dimensional VAR(1) companion system \(\mathbf{Z}_t = \mathbf{C} + \mathbf{F}\mathbf{Z}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}_t\). The system is weakly stationary if and only if all eigenvalues of the companion matrix \(\mathbf{F}\) have modulus strictly less than \(1\), equivalently: \[\det\left(\mathbf{I}_K - \sum_{i=1}^p \mathbf{\Phi}_i z^i\right) \neq 0, \quad \forall |z| \le 1 \tag{2.6}\]


3.4.3 Sample Problem 2.3 (Bivariate VAR(1) Stability & Forecasting)
Statement: Let \(\mathbf{Y}_t = \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.7 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{Y}_{t-1} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t\). Check stability and compute \(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{T+1|T}\) given \(\mathbf{Y}_T = [40, 100]^T\).
Solution: Eigenvalues satisfy \(\det(\mathbf{\Phi}_1 - \lambda \mathbf{I}) = (0.6-\lambda)(0.7-\lambda) - 0.02 = \lambda^2 - 1.3\lambda + 0.40 = (\lambda-0.8)(\lambda-0.5) = 0\). Since \(|\lambda_1|=0.8 < 1\) and \(|\lambda_2|=0.5 < 1\), the system is stable. Forecast: \(\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{T+1|T} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.6(40)+0.2(100) \\ 0.1(40)+0.7(100) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 44 \\ 74 \end{bmatrix}\).






Key Takeaway:



VAR(\(p\)) models capture bidirectional cross-channel feedback (such as brain-region connectivity or cross-asset spillovers) and enable formal Granger causality testing.

3.5 Conditional Heteroscedastic Models: ARCH and GARCH
Let \(r_t = \mu_t + a_t\) where \(a_t = \sigma_t \epsilon_t\), \(\epsilon_t \overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\), and \(\sigma_t^2 = \mathrm{Var}(r_t | \mathcal{F}_{t-1})\) is the time-varying conditional variance [1], [5], [6].

3.5.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

ARCH(\(q\)) (Engle, 1982): \(\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^q \alpha_i a_{t-i}^2\) (\(\alpha_0 > 0, \alpha_i \ge 0\)).
GARCH(\(p,q\)) (Bollerslev, 1986): \(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \sum_{i=1}^q \alpha_i a_{t-i}^2 + \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j \sigma_{t-j}^2\) (\(\omega > 0, \alpha_i, \beta_j \ge 0\)).
Volatility Persistence (\(\alpha + \beta\)): Governs how slowly a volatility spike decays back to the long-run variance \(\bar{\sigma}^2\).



3.5.2 First-Principles Derivations: ARCH(1) Kurtosis & GARCH(1,1) Persistence

3.5.2.1 Theorem 2.1: Unconditional Variance & Leptokurtosis of ARCH(1)
For \(\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 a_{t-1}^2\) with \(0 \le \alpha_1 < 1\) and \(3\alpha_1^2 < 1\): \[\bar{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\alpha_0}{1 - \alpha_1}, \qquad \kappa = \frac{\mathbb{E}[a_t^4]}{(\mathbb{E}[a_t^2])^2} = 3\frac{1 - \alpha_1^2}{1 - 3\alpha_1^2} > 3 \tag{2.7}\]
Derivation from First Principles: By the Law of Total Expectation, \(\mathbb{E}[a_t^2] = \mathbb{E}[\sigma_t^2 \mathbb{E}[\epsilon_t^2|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]] = \mathbb{E}[\sigma_t^2] = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1\mathbb{E}[a_{t-1}^2]\). Under stationarity (\(\mathbb{E}[a_t^2] = \bar{\sigma}^2\)), solving gives \(\bar{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\alpha_0}{1 - \alpha_1}\). For the fourth moment, since \(\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_t^4] = 3\): \[\mathbb{E}[a_t^4] = 3\mathbb{E}[\sigma_t^4] = 3\mathbb{E}\big[(\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 a_{t-1}^2)^2\big] = 3\alpha_0^2 + 6\alpha_0\alpha_1 \bar{\sigma}^2 + 3\alpha_1^2 \mathbb{E}[a_{t-1}^4]\] Substituting \(\bar{\sigma}^2 = \alpha_0/(1-\alpha_1)\) and solving for \(\mathbb{E}[a_t^4]\) yields \(\mathbb{E}[a_t^4] = \frac{3\alpha_0^2(1+\alpha_1)}{(1-\alpha_1)(1-3\alpha_1^2)}\). Dividing by \((\bar{\sigma}^2)^2 = \frac{\alpha_0^2}{(1-\alpha_1)^2}\) gives \(\kappa = 3\frac{1 - \alpha_1^2}{1 - 3\alpha_1^2} > 3\). Even with Normal innovations \(\epsilon_t\), ARCH generates fat tails!


3.5.2.2 Theorem 2.2: GARCH(1,1) Stationarity & Multi-Step Variance Forecast
For \(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha a_{t-1}^2 + \beta \sigma_{t-1}^2\), taking expectations gives \(\bar{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\omega}{1 - (\alpha + \beta)}\) (requiring \(\alpha + \beta < 1\)). Iterating \(k\) steps ahead: \[\mathbb{E}[\sigma_{t+k}^2 | \mathcal{F}_t] = \bar{\sigma}^2 + (\alpha + \beta)^{k-1}\big(\sigma_{t+1}^2 - \bar{\sigma}^2\big) \tag{2.8}\]



3.5.3 Sample Problem 2.4 (ARCH(1) Risk & Kurtosis)
Statement: A stock return series follows ARCH(1): \(\sigma_t^2 = 0.00004 + 0.35 a_{t-1}^2\). Compute \(\bar{\sigma}^2\), annualized volatility (\(\times\sqrt{252}\)), and theoretical kurtosis \(\kappa\).
Solution: \(\bar{\sigma}^2 = \frac{0.00004}{1 - 0.35} \approx 6.1538 \times 10^{-5}\). Annualized volatility: \(\sqrt{252 \times 6.1538\times 10^{-5}} \approx 12.45\%\). Since \(3(0.35)^2 = 0.3675 < 1\), \(\kappa = 3\frac{1 - 0.1225}{1 - 0.3675} \approx 4.162 > 3\) (leptokurtic).






Key Takeaway:



ARCH and GARCH model time-varying risk (\(\sigma_t^2\)), naturally explaining both volatility clustering and fat-tailed return distributions when \(\alpha + \beta < 1\).

3.6 3-Tier Graduated Problem Ladder

3.6.1 Tier 1: By-Hand Intuition

Problem 2.5 (Practice): Identify the orders \((p,d,q)\times(P,D,Q)_{12}\) of \((1 - 0.5B)(1 - B)(1 - B^{12})X_t = (1 + 0.3B^{12})Z_t\). (Answer: \(\mathrm{SARIMA}(1,1,0)\times(0,1,1)_{12}\).)
Problem 2.6 (Practice): A GARCH(1,1) has \(\omega = 2\times 10^{-6}\), \(\alpha = 0.09\), \(\beta = 0.89\). Compute the long-run daily volatility \(\bar{\sigma}\). (Answer: \(\bar{\sigma}^2 = 2\times 10^{-6}/0.02 = 0.0001 \implies \bar{\sigma} = 1.0\%\).)



3.6.2 Tier 2: Analytical & Exam-Style

Problem 2.7 (Worked — GARCH(1,1) as ARMA(1,1)): Show that \(a_t^2\) in GARCH(1,1) obeys an ARMA(1,1) equation. Solution: Let \(\nu_t = a_t^2 - \sigma_t^2\) (note \(\mathbb{E}[\nu_t|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}] = 0\)). Substituting \(\sigma_t^2 = a_t^2 - \nu_t\) into \(\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha a_{t-1}^2 + \beta \sigma_{t-1}^2\) gives \(a_t^2 - \nu_t = \omega + \alpha a_{t-1}^2 + \beta(a_{t-1}^2 - \nu_{t-1}) \implies a_t^2 = \omega + (\alpha + \beta)a_{t-1}^2 + \nu_t - \beta\nu_{t-1}\), which is ARMA(1,1) with \(\phi_1 = \alpha+\beta\) and \(\theta_1 = -\beta\).



3.6.3 Tier 3: Domain Case Studies (EEG & Finance/Portfolio)

Problem 2.8 (EEG Multi-Channel Granger Coupling — Worked): In a 2-channel EEG VAR(1) connecting Frontal (\(Y_{1,t}\)) and Occipital (\(Y_{2,t}\)) cortex, \(\mathbf{\Phi}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.0 \\ 0.35 & 0.4 \end{bmatrix}\). Does Occipital activity Granger-cause Frontal activity? Solution: Look at row 1, col 2: \(\Phi_{1,12} = 0.0\), so Occipital lags do not predict Frontal activity. However, \(\Phi_{1,21} = 0.35 \neq 0\), meaning Frontal activity unidirectionally Granger-causes Occipital activity.
Problem 2.9 (Dynamic Portfolio Value-at-Risk — Practice): Using Problem 2.6’s GARCH(1,1), today’s shock is \(a_T = -0.03\) (\(-3\%\)) and \(\sigma_T = 0.01\). Compute tomorrow’s 1-day 99% VaR (\(\text{VaR}_{0.99} = 2.326\,\sigma_{T+1}\)) for a Rs.10,00,000 portfolio. (Answer: \(\sigma_{T+1}^2 = 2\times 10^{-6} + 0.09(0.0009) + 0.89(0.0001) = 0.000172 \implies \sigma_{T+1} = 1.311\%\), \(\text{VaR}_{0.99} \approx 30,505\).)

3.7 Dual-Track Laboratory Experimental Section

3.7.1 Lab Track A: Multi-Channel EEG VAR(p) & Granger Connectivity
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR

# Simulate coupled 2-channel EEG (Frontal -> Occipital delayed propagation)
np.random.seed(10)
n = 600
frontal = np.zeros(n)
occipital = np.zeros(n)
e1, e2 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n), np.random.normal(0, 1, n)

for t in range(1, n):
    frontal[t] = 0.65 * frontal[t-1] + e1[t]
    occipital[t] = 0.45 * occipital[t-1] + 0.40 * frontal[t-1] + e2[t]

eeg_df = pd.DataFrame({"Frontal": frontal, "Occipital": occipital})
var_fit = VAR(eeg_df).fit(maxlags=2, ic="aic")
print(var_fit.summary())

# Test Granger causality: Does Frontal Granger-cause Occipital?
gc_f_to_o = var_fit.test_causality("Occipital", ["Frontal"], kind="f")
gc_o_to_f = var_fit.test_causality("Frontal", ["Occipital"], kind="f")
print(f"\nFrontal -> Occipital p-value: {gc_f_to_o.pvalue:.4e}")
print(f"Occipital -> Frontal p-value: {gc_o_to_f.pvalue:.4e}")


3.7.2 Lab Track B: SARIMA Forecasting & GARCH(1,1) Portfolio VaR
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX
from scipy.optimize import minimize

# Part 1: Box-Jenkins Airline SARIMA(0,1,1)x(0,1,1)_12
air = sm.datasets.get_rdataset("AirPassengers", package="datasets").data["value"]
log_air = np.log(pd.Series(air.values, index=pd.date_range("1949-01-01", periods=len(air), freq="MS")))
sarima = SARIMAX(log_air.iloc[:-12], order=(0, 1, 1), seasonal_order=(0, 1, 1, 12)).fit(disp=False)
pred = np.exp(sarima.get_forecast(12).predicted_mean)
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((np.exp(log_air.iloc[-12:]) - pred)**2))
print(f"Airline 12-Month Out-of-Sample RMSE: {rmse:.2f} thousand passengers")

# Part 2: GARCH(1,1) MLE & 99% VaR Backtest on Equity Returns
np.random.seed(42)
T = 1000
r, s2 = np.zeros(T), np.zeros(T)
s2[0] = 0.0001
eps = np.random.normal(0, 1, T)
for t in range(1, T):
    s2[t] = 0.00001 + 0.08 * r[t-1]**2 + 0.88 * s2[t-1]
    r[t] = np.sqrt(s2[t]) * eps[t]

def neg_ll(params):
    w, a, b = params
    if w <= 0 or a < 0 or b < 0 or a + b >= 1:
        return 1e10
    sig2 = np.empty(T)
    sig2[0] = np.var(r)
    for t in range(1, T):
        sig2[t] = w + a * r[t-1]**2 + b * sig2[t-1]
    return 0.5 * np.sum(np.log(2 * np.pi * sig2) + r**2 / sig2)

res = minimize(neg_ll, [0.00002, 0.1, 0.8], method="Nelder-Mead")
w_hat, a_hat, b_hat = res.x
print(f"GARCH(1,1) MLE -> omega={w_hat:.6f}, alpha={a_hat:.4f}, beta={b_hat:.4f}, persistence={a_hat+b_hat:.4f}")

3.8 Summary of Concepts

ARMA(\(p,q\)): Combines AR and MA polynomials; valid identification requires no common factors and all roots outside \(|z| > 1\).
ARIMA & SARIMA: First and seasonal differencing (\(\nabla^d \nabla_s^D\)) eliminate unit roots and periodic trends without over-differencing.

ARCH / GARCH: Models time-varying conditional variance \(\sigma_t^2\), producing volatility clustering, fat tails (\(\kappa > 3\)), and dynamic Value-at-Risk bounds.

4.1 Nonlinear Asymmetry and Apollo’s Navigation Filter
Every stationary Gaussian linear model is time-reversible: if you play an AR(2) trajectory backward in time, its statistical moments look identical [1]. Yet real-world systems are fiercely asymmetric. Stock markets climb slowly over years of bull runs and crash vertically in weeks; epileptic EEG spikes rise abruptly and decay slowly; predator-prey populations (like Howell Tong’s famous Canadian Lynx data) build gradually and collapse suddenly [6]. In 1980, Tong broke the linear barrier with Threshold Autoregressive (TAR) models, allowing system dynamics to switch regimes across physical thresholds.
At the same time, Rudolf Kalman (1960) revolutionized tracking by separating the unobserved true physical state (a spacecraft’s orbit, a patient’s true cortical potential, or a stock’s latent beta) from noisy sensor measurements [2], [5]. Embedded in the Apollo Guidance Computer, the Kalman filter remains the gold standard for real-time filtering and smoothing.

text:
4.2 Nonlinear Time Series: SETAR and STAR

4.2.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

Time Irreversibility: Statistical asymmetry between forward (\(X_1, \dots, X_T\)) and reversed (\(X_T, \dots, X_1\)) paths—impossible in Gaussian linear models.
SETAR(\(k; p_1, \dots, p_k\)): Self-Exciting Threshold Autoregressive model where regime \(j\) activates when lag \(X_{t-d}\) falls in \((r_{j-1}, r_j]\) [6]: \[X_t = \sum_{j=1}^k \left(\phi_0^{(j)} + \sum_{i=1}^{p_j} \phi_i^{(j)} X_{t-i} + \sigma^{(j)} Z_t\right) \mathbb{I}(r_{j-1} < X_{t-d} \le r_j) \tag{3.1}\]
Smooth Transition AR (STAR): Replaces the hard indicator step with a smooth logistic transition \(G(X_{t-d}; \gamma, c) = \big[1 + \exp(-\gamma(X_{t-d}-c))\big]^{-1} \in (0,1)\).



4.2.2 First-Principles Insight: Asymmetric Limit Cycles in SETAR(2;1,1)
Consider a 2-regime system with threshold \(r = 3.0\): \[X_t = \begin{cases} 0.5 + 0.85 X_{t-1} + Z_t, & X_{t-1} \le 3.0 \\ 6.0 - 0.40 X_{t-1} + Z_t, & X_{t-1} > 3.0 \end{cases}\] In Regime 1, the deterministic fixed point \(x_1^* = 0.5/(1-0.85) = 3.333\) lies above the threshold \(3.0\), pushing \(X_t\) upward until it crosses \(3.0\). Once above \(3.0\), Regime 2 takes over with negative slope \(-0.40\), snapping the state back down—generating self-sustaining asymmetric cycles.


4.2.3 Sample Problem 3.1 (Tracing a SETAR Deterministic Skeleton)
Statement: Starting from \(X_0 = 2.8\) with \(Z_t = 0\), compute \(X_1, X_2, X_3\) for the SETAR model above.
Solution:

\(X_0 = 2.8 \le 3.0 \implies X_1 = 0.5 + 0.85(2.8) = 2.88\).
\(X_1 = 2.88 \le 3.0 \implies X_2 = 0.5 + 0.85(2.88) = 2.948\).
\(X_2 = 2.948 \le 3.0 \implies X_3 = 0.5 + 0.85(2.948) = 3.0058 > 3.0\) (crosses threshold into Regime 2 on the next step!).







Key Takeaway:



SETAR and STAR models capture regime-dependent slopes, volatility asymmetry, and limit cycles that linear ARMA models cannot reproduce.

4.3 Formal Hypothesis Tests for Stationarity
Visual ACF inspection can mislead. So we pair two complementary unit-root tests to form a confirmatory stationarity matrix [1], [4].

4.3.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) Test: Tests \(H_0: \gamma = 0\) (Unit Root / Non-Stationary) against \(H_1: \gamma < 0\) (Stationary) in: \[\Delta X_t = \alpha + \beta t + \gamma X_{t-1} + \sum_{i=1}^p \psi_i \Delta X_{t-i} + e_t \tag{3.2}\] Under \(H_0\), \(t_\gamma = \hat{\gamma}/\mathrm{SE}(\hat{\gamma})\) follows the non-standard Dickey-Fuller Brownian motion distribution, which has much more negative critical values than Student’s \(t\) [7].
Phillips-Perron (PP) Test: Non-parametric alternative to ADF using Newey-West HAC variance correction instead of lagged \(\Delta X_{t-i}\) terms.
KPSS Test (1992): Reverses the hypotheses! \(H_0\): Stationary (\(\sigma_u^2 = 0\) in random-walk component) vs. \(H_1\): Unit Root, using \(LM = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^T S_t^2}{T^2 s^2(l)}\) where \(S_t = \sum_{i=1}^t e_i\) [8].

4.3.3 Sample Problem 3.2 (ADF Statistic Evaluation)
Statement: An OLS fit yields \(\Delta X_t = -0.15 X_{t-1} + 0.25 \Delta X_{t-1} + e_t\) with \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat{\gamma}) = 0.05\) (\(5\%\) DF critical value \(= -1.95\)). Test for a unit root.
Solution: \(ADF = \frac{-0.15}{0.05} = -3.00\). Since \(-3.00 < -1.95\) (deeper in the left tail), we reject \(H_0\) and conclude the series is stationary.






Key Takeaway:



Always run ADF and KPSS together: ADF checks if a unit root can be rejected, while KPSS checks if stationarity can be rejected.

text:
4.4 Formal Hypothesis Tests for Nonlinearity
Before abandoning linear models, we test whether linear ARMA residuals \(\hat{e}_t\) still hide nonlinear structure [1], [2].

4.4.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms

McLeod-Li Test: Applies the Ljung-Box portmanteau statistic to squared residuals \(\hat{e}_t^2\): \[Q_{ML} = T(T+2)\sum_{k=1}^M \frac{\hat{r}_{ee}^2(k)}{T - k} \sim \chi^2(M) \tag{3.3}\] Rejection indicates ARCH effects or quadratic nonlinearity.
Keenan’s & Tsay’s Tests: Regress \(X_t\) on squared fitted values \(\hat{X}_t^2\) (Keenan) or all cross-products \(X_{t-i}X_{t-j}\) (Tsay) via an \(F\)-test.
BDS Test: Uses correlation integrals \(C_m(\epsilon, T)\) from chaos theory; under \(i.i.d.\) residuals, \(W_m = \sqrt{T}\frac{C_m - C_1^m}{\hat{\sigma}_m} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1)\).



4.4.2 Sample Problem 3.3 (McLeod-Li Decision)
Statement: An AR(1) fit to \(T=200\) stock returns leaves uncorrelated residuals \(\hat{e}_t\), but \(Q_{ML}\) at lag \(M=10\) is \(34.2\) (\(\chi^2_{0.95}(10) = 18.31\)). What do you conclude?
Solution: Since \(34.2 > 18.31\), we reject linearity/\(i.i.d.\) residuals and diagnose significant conditional heteroscedasticity (ARCH/GARCH) or nonlinear dependence.






Key Takeaway:



Linear white residuals (\(\hat{\rho}_e(k) \approx 0\)) do not guarantee independence; McLeod-Li and BDS detect hidden nonlinear or volatility structure.

text:
4.5 State-Space Models and the Kalman Filter
A State-Space Model (SSM) separates latent physical dynamics from noisy observations [2], [5].

4.5.1 Key Definitions & Important Terms






Definition 3.1: Linear Gaussian State-Space Model



\[\begin{aligned}
\text{State Equation:} \quad \mathbf{x}_t &= \mathbf{\Phi}_t \mathbf{x}_{t-1} + \mathbf{w}_t, & \mathbf{w}_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_t) \\
\text{Observation Equation:} \quad \mathbf{y}_t &= \mathbf{A}_t \mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{v}_t, & \mathbf{v}_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{R}_t)
\end{aligned} \tag{3.4}\]



Filtering (\(\mathbf{x}_{t|t}\)) vs. Smoothing (\(\mathbf{x}_{t|T}\)): Filtering estimates the state using data up to \(t\); smoothing (Rauch-Tung-Striebel) uses the entire record \([1, T]\).



4.5.2 First-Principles Derivation of the Optimal Kalman Gain \(\mathbf{K}_t\)
Let \(\mathbf{x}_{t|t-1} = \mathbf{\Phi}_t \mathbf{x}_{t-1|t-1}\) and \(\mathbf{P}_{t|t-1} = \mathbf{\Phi}_t \mathbf{P}_{t-1|t-1}\mathbf{\Phi}_t^T + \mathbf{Q}_t\) be the prior prediction and covariance. When \(\mathbf{y}_t\) arrives, the innovation is \(\boldsymbol{\nu}_t = \mathbf{y}_t - \mathbf{A}_t \mathbf{x}_{t|t-1}\) with covariance \(\mathbf{F}_t = \mathbf{A}_t \mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}\mathbf{A}_t^T + \mathbf{R}_t\).
We update the state linearly: \(\mathbf{x}_{t|t} = \mathbf{x}_{t|t-1} + \mathbf{K}_t \boldsymbol{\nu}_t\). The posterior error is \(\mathbf{e}_t = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_t \mathbf{A}_t)(\mathbf{x}_t - \mathbf{x}_{t|t-1}) - \mathbf{K}_t \mathbf{v}_t\), giving posterior covariance: \[\mathbf{P}_{t|t} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_t \mathbf{A}_t)\mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_t \mathbf{A}_t)^T + \mathbf{K}_t \mathbf{R}_t \mathbf{K}_t^T \tag{3.5}\] Differentiating \(\mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf{P}_{t|t})\) with respect to \(\mathbf{K}_t\) and setting to zero: \[\frac{\partial \mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf{P}_{t|t})}{\partial \mathbf{K}_t} = -2(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_t\mathbf{A}_t)\mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}\mathbf{A}_t^T + 2\mathbf{K}_t\mathbf{R}_t = \mathbf{0} \implies \mathbf{K}_t(\mathbf{A}_t\mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}\mathbf{A}_t^T + \mathbf{R}_t) = \mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}\mathbf{A}_t^T\] \[\mathbf{K}_t = \mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}\mathbf{A}_t^T \mathbf{F}_t^{-1}, \qquad \mathbf{P}_{t|t} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_t\mathbf{A}_t)\mathbf{P}_{t|t-1} \tag{3.6}\]


4.5.3 Sample Problem 3.4 (1D Scalar Kalman Filter Update)
Statement: Let \(x_t = 0.9 x_{t-1} + w_t\) (\(Q=4\)) and \(y_t = x_t + v_t\) (\(R=2\)). Given \(x_{0|0} = 10\), \(P_{0|0} = 5\), and \(y_1 = 12\), compute \(x_{1|1}\) and \(P_{1|1}\).
Solution:

Predict: \(x_{1|0} = 0.9(10) = 9.0\); \(P_{1|0} = 0.9^2(5) + 4 = 8.05\).
Innovation: \(\nu_1 = 12 - 9.0 = 3.0\); \(F_1 = 8.05 + 2 = 10.05\).
Gain: \(K_1 = 8.05 / 10.05 \approx 0.8010\).
Update: \(x_{1|1} = 9.0 + 0.8010(3.0) \approx 11.403\); \(P_{1|1} = (1 - 0.8010)(8.05) \approx 1.602\).







Key Takeaway: Section 3.5



The Kalman gain \(\mathbf{K}_t\) automatically balances trust between the physical state model (\(\mathbf{P}_{t|t-1}\)) and incoming sensor measurements (\(\mathbf{R}_t\)).

4.6 3-Tier Graduated Problem Ladder

4.6.1 Tier 1: By-Hand Intuition

Problem 3.5 (Practice): In a scalar Local Level model (\(x_t = x_{t-1} + w_t\), \(Q=1\), \(R=9\)), if \(P_{1|0} = 3\), compute \(K_1\). (Answer: \(K_1 = 3/(3+9) = 0.25\) — low trust in noisy sensor.)
Problem 3.6 (Practice): An ADF test gives \(p = 0.42\) and KPSS gives \(p = 0.01\). What is the diagnosis? (Answer: Non-stationary unit root; first-difference the series.)



4.6.2 Tier 2: Analytical & Exam-Style

Problem 3.7 (Worked — Local Linear Trend State Matrices): Write \(\mathbf{\Phi}\) and \(\mathbf{A}\) for \(y_t = \mu_t + \epsilon_t\), \(\mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + \eta_t\), \(\beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + \zeta_t\). Solution: Setting \(\mathbf{x}_t = [\mu_t, \beta_t]^T\), we get \(\mathbf{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).



4.6.3 Tier 3: Domain Case Studies (EEG & Finance)

Problem 3.8 (EEG Kalman Denoising — Worked): An EEG electrode suffers sudden motion-artifact noise (\(R\) jumps from \(2\) to \(50\) \(\mu\text{V}^2\)) while \(P_{t|t-1} = 4\). How does \(K_t\) react? Solution: \(K_t\) drops from \(4/(4+2) = 0.67\) down to \(4/(4+50) = 0.074\), automatically shielding the latent cortical estimate from the noisy spike.
Problem 3.9 (Dynamic CAPM Beta via Kalman Filter — Practice): Formulate a stock’s excess return \(y_t = \beta_t r_{m,t} + v_t\) where latent beta follows a random walk \(\beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + w_t\). Identify \(\mathbf{\Phi}_t\) and \(\mathbf{A}_t\). (Answer: \(\Phi_t = 1\), time-varying observation matrix \(A_t = r_{m,t}\).)

4.7 Dual-Track Laboratory Experimental Section

4.7.1 Lab Track A: EEG Denoising via Kalman Filtering & Smoothing
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.structural import UnobservedComponents
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox

# Simulate latent cortical potential + heavy electrode measurement noise
np.random.seed(7)
T = 300
t = np.arange(T)
true_eeg = 12 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 25) + np.cumsum(np.random.normal(0, 0.3, T))
noisy_eeg = true_eeg + np.random.normal(0, 4.0, T)

# Fit Local Level State-Space Model & extract Kalman Filtered / RTS Smoothed states
ssm = UnobservedComponents(noisy_eeg, level="local level").fit(disp=False)
print(f"Estimated Measurement Var R: {ssm.params['sigma2.measurement']:.2f}")
print(f"RMSE Raw Noisy: {np.sqrt(np.mean((noisy_eeg - true_eeg)**2)):.2f}")
print(f"RMSE RTS Smoothed: {np.sqrt(np.mean((ssm.smoothed_state[0] - true_eeg)**2)):.2f}")

# McLeod-Li test on standardized residuals
std_res = ssm.resid / np.sqrt(ssm.params["sigma2.measurement"])
print("\nMcLeod-Li Nonlinearity Test:\n", acorr_ljungbox(std_res**2, lags=[5, 10], return_df=True))


4.7.2 Lab Track B: Confirmatory Stationarity & Structural Breaks on Nile / Financial Levels
import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller, kpss

nile = sm.datasets.nile.load_pandas().data["volume"]
adf_stat, adf_p, *_ = adfuller(nile, autolag="AIC")
kpss_stat, kpss_p, *_ = kpss(nile, regression="c", nlags="auto")

print(f"Nile Flow -> ADF p={adf_p:.4f} | KPSS p={kpss_p:.4f}")
# Difference once and re-run Confirmatory Matrix
d_nile = nile.diff().dropna()
print(f"Differenced -> ADF p={adfuller(d_nile)[1]:.4e} | KPSS p={kpss(d_nile, nlags='auto')[1]:.4f}")

5.1 From Neural Gates to Planetary Tipping Points
Modern telemetry—multi-channel clinical EEGs, algorithmic limit-order books, and smart-grid sensors—generates millions of correlated sequences where manual ARIMA identification cannot scale [1]. Reframing forecasting as supervised learning via delay-coordinate embeddings, tree ensembles (Random Forests, GBDT), recurrent gates (LSTM/GRU) [6], dilated TCNs, and causal Transformers unlocked non-linear, multi-horizon predictive analytics across both biomedical signals and quantitative finance.
Yet standard forecasting faces a deeper challenge: catastrophic regime shifts (epileptic seizures, financial flash crashes, ecosystem collapses) where history offers few or no prior examples of the crash [5]. In 2009, Marten Scheffer et al. proved that as any nonlinear system approaches a tipping point, its recovery rate from small perturbations slows down—a universal phenomenon called Critical Slowing Down (CSD) that leaves clear statistical fingerprints (\(\rho(1) \to 1\) and surging variance) long before collapse.
